401.quote_or_event: “Wisdom which leads to arguments is not called wisdom. Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
401.explanation: In a salok of the Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak denies the name of wisdom to cleverness spent in disputation and says that real wisdom serves God and is what earns honour.
401.tie_back: The Kural mocks the man who enters a learned assembly to argue without having mastered his texts; Guru Nanak likewise says that argument without true understanding is not wisdom and brings no honour.
401.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
401._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both reject empty debating, but the Kural prizes mastery of texts, while in the same salok (as Sant Singh Khalsa renders it) Gurbani says wisdom does not come from reading textbooks.

402.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
402.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak, speaking as the soul-bride, admits the gap between fine words and poor conduct.
402.tie_back: The Kural ridicules the unlearned man who longs to be admired for his speech; Guru Nanak likewise exposes speech that has nothing real behind it.
402.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
402._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared theme is speech without substance, but Guru Nanak contrasts words with conduct rather than with learning, and the Kural's harsh simile has no Gurbani counterpart.

403.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
403.explanation: In Raag Dhanaasree Guru Nanak warns that much talking turns into idle babble.
403.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned keep their worth only by keeping quiet before the learned; Guru Nanak likewise counts excess speech as worthless.
403.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
403._accuracy_note: Partial: Gurbani values restraint in speech, but this line addresses everyone and is not about the unlearned keeping silent before scholars.

404.quote_or_event: “Hundreds of thousands of clever tricks, but not even one of them will go along with you in the end.”
404.explanation: In the first pauri of Japji Sahib Guru Nanak says that no amount of cleverness carries a person through to God.
404.tie_back: The Kural says the wise will not accept the cleverness of the unlearned, however striking; Guru Nanak says cleverness without true understanding does not hold up at all.
404.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
404._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both distrust mere cleverness, but Guru Nanak contrasts it with surrender to God's hukam, not with formal learning.

405.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, egotism is eliminated.”
405.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan lists the fruits of the Saadh Sangat and says pride dissolves in the company of the holy.
405.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned man's self-esteem withers when he meets the learned; Guru Arjan says self-importance is undone in the company of the truly wise and holy.
405.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
405._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both describe pride shrinking in good company, but Guru Arjan treats this as a blessing that cures haumai, not as the humiliation of an unlearned man.

406.quote_or_event: “The evil-minded ones plant their seed in the barren soil; such is the sign of those who have no Guru.”
406.explanation: In Raag Malaar Guru Nanak uses the image of seed sown in barren, saline soil for the effort of those without the Guru's guidance.
406.tie_back: The Kural compares the unlearned to barren saline land that yields nothing; Guru Nanak uses the same image of barren soil (kalar) for a life without the Guru's teaching.
406.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1275, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
406._accuracy_note: A strong fit: the same image of barren saline soil, though for Guru Nanak what is missing is the Guru's guidance rather than book-learning.

407.quote_or_event: “The simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
407.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak describes the simmal (silk-cotton) tree, impressive to look at but giving nothing of use.
407.tie_back: The Kural likens a handsome person without subtle understanding to a painted clay doll; Guru Nanak's tall, fine-looking but fruitless simmal tree makes the same point about outward show without inner worth.
407.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
407._accuracy_note: A strong fit on fine appearance without substance; in the salok the missing quality is sweetness and humility rather than learning.

408.quote_or_event: “Even poverty is bliss, if God comes to mind in the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy.”
408.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Arjan says that poverty is joyful when it is lived in holy company with God in mind.
408.tie_back: The Kural says poverty falling on the good is less painful than wealth in the hands of the unlearned; Guru Arjan likewise says poverty with God in mind is bliss.
408.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 745, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
408._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it supports the half of the Kural about the good poor, but says nothing about wealth held by the unlearned.

409.quote_or_event: “No one should be proud of his social class and status. He alone is a Brahmin, who knows God.”
409.explanation: In Raag Bhairao Guru Amar Das rejects pride of caste and says that true standing comes from knowing God, not from birth.
409.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned high-born are worth less than the learned low-born; Guru Amar Das goes further, denying any worth to birth and placing it in knowledge of God.
409.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1127, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
409._accuracy_note: Near match: both rank knowledge above birth, though the Kural ranks within a caste order while Sikh teaching rejects caste altogether, and the knowledge it values is knowledge of God.

410.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
410.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan describes people who are human in form but beast-like in conduct.
410.tie_back: The Kural says the unlearned compare with the learned as beasts with humans; Guru Arjan uses the same human-and-beast contrast.
410.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
410._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the human-versus-beast contrast; Guru Arjan bases it on conduct and spiritual blindness rather than lack of study.
